question: A programme team asks Claude to condense forty stakeholder interview transcripts into a single requirements list, then plans to send that list to a supplier as the final agreed scope without further review. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The supplier may raise follow-up questions that the programme team cannot answer without rereading material.
B) Working through forty long transcripts may take several minutes and consume a large share of the team's usage.
C) Needs raised in only one interview may be lost, and nobody has checked the list against the transcripts.
D) The list may be written as flowing prose when the supplier's template expects a numbered table of items.
correct_answers: C) Needs raised in only one interview may be lost, and nobody has checked the list against the transcripts.
explanations: Follow-up questions from a supplier are normal in any scoping exercise and are answerable by returning to the material. This is an inconvenience rather than the central danger of treating an unverified summary as agreed scope.

Processing time and usage consumption are real but recoverable costs. They do not affect the correctness of the scope being sent out, and they would not survive a comparison with a defect that only surfaces after the supplier has started building.

Correct. Summarising forty transcripts naturally favours what was said repeatedly, so a genuine but rarely voiced requirement can quietly disappear. Because the list becomes contractual scope with no verification pass against the sources, an omission is both likely and expensive to discover later.

Formatting is a presentation issue that is trivially fixed by asking for a different layout. It has no bearing on whether the scope the supplier is being asked to build is actually the scope the stakeholders described.
